speechtext: wish to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the widespread interest in the announcement the minister made the day before yesterday about certain Canadian economic guide lines, I should like to ask the hon. gentleman whether these guide lines will cover the securities of Canadian subsidiaries of United States corporations and, if not, why no attempt is being made to block this loophole by means of which capital could be raised in Canada for investment in third countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUIDE LINES-INSTRUCTIONS TO U.S. SUBSIDIARIES
speechtext:
I am not certain that I completely understood the question put by the hon. gentleman. In the announcement I made the other day I was concerned with the possible flow of capital from Canada and, therefore, from North America, because of our access to the American market, to be used in foreign countries for the financing of foreign projects. It seemed to us that my request was in the national interest as a means of defending not only the Canadian capital market but the North American capital market. As I said at the time, this was done after discussion with the United States; indeed, the United States itself welcomed those measures.
We did not feel it was necessary to go any further than that at the present time. As far as Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies are concerned, companies which might be raising money in this market, it was believed-and this belief has now been strengthened as a result of discussions we had with the United States when Canadian cabinet ministers met with United States secretaries-that Canadian subsidiaries would act in a normal way and as good Canadian citizens.
Therefore, as I said, we did not feel there was any loophole to be plugged. I would add, however, that the government is giving consideration to reinforcing the advice which has been given to these companies as a result of the discussions we had in Washington, by trying to define what constitutes good Canadian citizenship on the part of subsidiaries.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, March 17, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Drury-Mr. Batten in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure for the establishment of a Science Council of Canada and to define the duties thereof, to provide for the appointment of the chairman and other members of the council and for the payment of the remuneration of the chairman and of travelling expenses of the members and associate members of the council, also for the payment of the remuneration of members of the council for additional duties: to provide further that all expenditures for the purposes of this measure shall be paid out of money appropriated by parliament therefor.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like a few more minutes to conclude the remarks I was making last evening on this resolution.
I was saying, Mr. Chairman, just before the ten o'clock adjournment that the effort being put by the Canadian government into science research, and indeed the support of our academic centres vis-a-vis science research, did not compare very well with the effort put into this same field by the governments of other industrial nations. I concluded my remarks by reading into the record a letter which I believe could be typical of the attitude of many of our graduate students when they find themselves having to move to the United States; not so much because the salaries are better, although that is one reason, but usually because there is greater opportunity for them in their chosen scientific careers across the border.
It is often said, Mr. Chairman, that when making a comparison between Canada and the United States the ratio which should be used is ten to one; that whatever is being done in the United States should be achieved by Canada in the order of one tenth of the accomplishment. Now, it is true that sometimes comparisons are odious and invidious, but from time to time it is necessary for us to make comparisons in order to see how we measure up to progress and efforts made by other nations. When one compares the efforts in our Canadian graduate schools with the United States graduate schools, we find we are lagging behind.
March 18, 1966	COMMONS
I have some data, Mr. Chairman, which I believe will be of interest. This is taken from the first report of the Economic Council of Canada, and the report makes the observation that Canadian universities produce one doctoral degree for every 33 degrees granted in the United States. This is entirely out of proportion to our population ratio and is out of proportion to our national income levels, Mr. Chairman. Therefore on both counts it is fairly obvious that we are lagging behind in so far as science research effort is concerned.
Some sources put the ratio in the order of $100 expended on science research in the United States, both at the universities and in industry, while only $1 is expended in Canadian research, which is a fantastic discrepancy, Mr. Chairman. This ratio, if allowed to continue for long, will simply mean that with each passing year our rate of economic growth and industrial productivity will continue to lag behind even more the advanced and developed nations.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that in addition to a science advisory council, which is now before us, the government should seriously consider greater financial support to our major universities which will enable them to expand their graduate school science research programs. This is not all that should be done with regard to our university graduate research centres. This government should also be assisting industry in expanding its science research capability, which may have to be done on a co-operative basis.
Last year, for example, the Ontario Research Foundation recommended the establishment in this country of a system of research associations integrated at the national level for the purpose of undertaking research for companies within industrial fields. These industrial research associations could presumably be integrated and co-ordinated by the federal government, and if necessary the federal government could establish a crown corporation with somewhat the same purpose as the Rand Corporation in the United States, a publicly owned think factory, if you like, which in addition to carrying out its own science research could also act as a co-ordinating agency for a system of research associations in different parts of the country.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
Whatever approach is adopted, one thing that is clear is that the government of Canada must certainly do a good deal more than it has done up to now in providing 23033-181J

Science Council oj Canada leadership and a means of co-ordinating our research efforts, as well as in providing a greater degree of financial support.
We find when making comparisons between our effort here and that in other countries, so far as industrial science is concerned, that Canada compares very poorly indeed. I have before me a chart published by the Ontario Research Foundation and which was later published in a Canadian electronics periodical in September last year. This chart shows that a small industrial nation like Belgium, for example, is able to sustain 55 industrial research associations, to support which the industrial firms pay up to 60 per cent of the cost with the government paying 30 per cent. In West Germany there are 61 industrial research co-ordinating associations or agencies, if you like, again with industry supporting over 60 per cent of the cost and the government over 30 per cent. In Sweden there are 27 such research associations with industry paying 75 per cent of the cost and the government over 20 per cent.
How does Canada compare, Mr. Chairman? Canada has two such industrial research associations which, according to this chart, are entirely supported by industry; there is no government support. Of course in relatively recent times the government has given some assistance to industrial research by way of tax write-offs and concessions, so we are making some progress.
It is pretty difficult to make a precise forecast, Mr. Chairman, without going into a great deal of detail, but one thing which does become eminently clear as we delve into this subject more and more is this. Science research in our academic graduate schools is not being supported by the government of this country to a sufficient degree, and our effort compares poorly with the effort put forth by other countries. In addition, the research carried on in our academic institutions and in Canadian industry leaves a great deal to be desired, not in terms of quality, Mr. Chairman, but in terms of personnel and actual quantity of programs being undertaken.
With those remarks, Mr. Chairman, I will conclude at this time, although I think it must be pointed out once again to the minister and to this administration that we can talk all we like about industrial productivity, but when our industrial research is lagging behind other exporting countries not only are we not going to make up any lag or deficiency; we will slip further behind.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief. We welcome the proposal to set up a science council and its proposed function as an advisory body. We also appreciate the outline of its duties presented to us by the minister last evening, when he spoke of it having the task of defining long range objectives in science for Canada, when he spoke of developing principles in research, and when he spoke of philosophy. Possibly he should have introduced an additional word at that time, because some of the most important decisions which will have to be taken in science research in the very immediate future will be moral ones.
There are a variety of aspects of scientific research which will increasingly concern the people of Canada. We trust that one of the functions of this advisory body will be to give immediate consideration to some of these issues. As an example of what I am talking about I might mention the proposals to synthesize various viruses, which could have far reaching implications for the future of human life on earth. That is only one of a great many problems.
I think we can trust the science council- and I believe that here we are talking primarily about the science council-to give good advice to the government as far as increasing our scientific research and providing opportunities in Canada for Canadian scientists. 1 think the council will give that kind of advice. These are the things which must be done, the things which are obvious, and we can expect them to give proper advice there.
The really difficult problems will arise when they come to questions of philosophy and morality in scientific research. The right answers will not always be obvious and their work will be difficult indeed. The members who compose the council will have to be chosen with the utmost care so we will have a group which will be able to give the best advice possible to the government on some of the extremely pressing problems which will come up in the future.
I prepared my remarks originally, Mr. Chairman, expecting the resolutions to be introduced the other way around, so I will have more to say on government order No. 4 when it comes up for debate.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution before the committee is seeking to attain very worthwhile objectives.
The minister said last night in his statement that the science council would try to define long term objectives for science in Canada, including all natural sciences as well as pure and applied sciences. He also assured the house that this would be an advisory body which would only advise the government by encouraging the development of science in Canada.
I have listened to the remarks made by hon. members in the house since the minister spoke.
It is very easy to see, in the light of the opinions expressed, that this new science council of Canada is expected to take an interest in a variety of fields, namely security, public health, natural resources, productivity, education and university programs.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are fields which, in my humble opinion-and I am not afraid to be considered narrow-minded-do not come, in
2868	COMMONS
Science Council of Canada the last analysis, under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
For many years, within the federal administration, I am not questioning their integrity but they have been trying to look after everything, and when they cannot come in through the front door, they do it by the back door. All indirect means are used to succeed, after a number of years and indirect precedents created here and there, in getting into fields which the Canadian constitution gave exclusively to the provinces.
Today the government wants to set up a national advisory science council. We are told: It is not going against the authority of the constitution, it is not invading the provincial field with regard to culture and education. It is only an advisory body.
But that is just it, Mr. Chairman, what advice will that body give? It will say to the federal government: It would be advisable to increase the expenditures of the federal government for grants to the universities, increased laboratory facilities, special studies, either in natural sciences or pure sciences.
The federal government will be advised to deal with matters which do not come under its jurisdiction under the Canadian constitution.
I know very well, Mr. Chairman, that when some hon. members talk of respecting the constitution, others look at them, curious, amused, saying that we are singing a tune which is utterly out of date.
But I feel that this way of doing things increases and multiplies tensions across Canada. If that is what is called co-operative federalism, I fail to see where the co-operation comes in.
For instance, have the ministers of the present government discussed with the provincial governments, at recent federal-provincial conferences on poverty or other topics, the creation of a national science council? No. A move is made, a field is entered into, and when one is strongly entrenched in it, when public funds have been spent in fields which are not allotted by the constitution to the central government, then the provinces are told: "Now, if you wish, we will co-operate".
So that is co-operative federalism? Well, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I respect that way of doing things, which has become desirable for nine provinces in Canada-I am the first to respect 1966 concepts of thought and action-but it does not reflect in any way the wishes and aspirations of Quebec and French Canada.
DEBATES	March 18, 1966
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I say that by invading this field, through that body, we are directly, or indirectly if you wish, dealing with the fields of education and culture which, according to the Canadian constitution, come strictly under provincial jurisdiction.
I have neither the time nor the intention of developing today all the arguments that prove that the federal government has, in the last few years, intruded into sectors which do not fall within its jurisdiction. I shall merely refer the house to Vol. II, Part III, page 237 of the French version of the Tremblay Commission report, where fair and profuse answers are given to the arguments developed here in the house, and elsewhere by other people, to justify the federal government's intrusion, not only in the field of science but in all spheres.
Specific answers are given to those arguments and I urge members of the house to study the arguments put forward in answer to the following contentions with regard to the theory of ancillary powers.
The argument concerning the financial incapacity of the provinces is often heard: Ottawa will look after this, Ottawa will be in a position to help the country for the common good, because the provinces do not have the financial means to do so. It is very easy to understand, since the argument is fully explained. The provinces are unable to deal adequately, in their universities and high schools, with the development of science because the central government keeps too great a share of tax revenue in the country. It is as simple as that. That is why the central government, while not handing over to the provinces an adequate share of tax revenue, intrudes in all types of fields in which constitutional responsibility is not too well defined.
At page 237 of the same report, extensive answers are also given to four other arguments: the distinction between culture and education, the right of the government to concern itself with education, the requirements of the common good, the national role and the needs of universities.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to summarize all this, but hon. members who want to know why Quebec has always been very sensitive about this matter will find here substantial arguments in this connection.
Therefore, I say that the creation of a Science Council of Canada is a unilateral and indirect intrusion in the field of education. It reflects the centralizing principle which has

March 18, 1986	COMMONS
been applied here in Ottawa for many years, whatever governments came into power, to the effect, for instance, that Ottawa enjoys an unlimited taxation power and an absolute power to spend in its own way. But that is not true. I say that this way of proceeding infringes the federalist nature of the Canadian constitution.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, even though I understand that the situation and mentalities have undergone great changes since 1867, I submit that we are today confronted with two mentalities: the English Canadian mentality, which does not object to the fact that the central government becomes interested in all sorts of fields, such as sciences, culture, scholarships, federal loans to students and, on the other hand, the French Canadian mentality, which does not want Ottawa to be the centre of all these activities and claims jealously provincial autonomy in these important and fundamental matters.
Mr. Chairman, decisions will have to be made one of these days because of those two attitudes.
The provinces cannot be suffered to invade a jurisdiction which possibly comes under the federal nor can the latter encroach without previous consultation, agreement or constitutional reform upon a provincial jurisdiction.
We are all hugger-muggering along, creating constitutional chaos and permanent tensions in the country.
I see that the government has again been sinking into lethargy during the past month and a half.
We have asked several members on both sides of the house to set up a parliamentary committee on constitutional reform to open a dialogue, to consider the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments in the economic and social context of 1966.
Other members have asked that this parliamentary committee appoint federal legislators who would define their views together, as a prelude to a national constitutional conference bringing together representatives of the provinces and federal legislators.

Mr. Chairman, not a single hon. member could disagree with the sentiments expressed by the minister when he introduced this resolution yesterday. In view of the complaints which have been made, not only from year to year but literally from week to week, by members of the scientific community, by physicists, by the medical profession, by chemists, by agricultural scientists, and by industrial researchers about the lack of direction in scientific policies, about the amount of money provided, about the woeful lack of support for all these disciplines from Canadian governments during the last ten years, it is obvious that this kind of organization is needed.
But, Mr. Chairman, as I read the minister's remarks in Hansard this morning I could not help thinking I have heard this before. It is practically word for word the same speech the Prime Minister made when he announced the formation of a scientific secretariat to be headed by Dr. Forward. I think that was two years ago. Since then we have allocated a little more money for scientific research than we provided previously, but basically nothing has changed. Our scientists are still complaining, and legitimately so, about the lack of

support from government. Basically they still do not know in what fields we are to concentrate our efforts, if we are to concentrate them at all. They do not know how much support they can get or expect from the government.
One thing this new organization can do, although on the basis of experience I am sceptical that it will, is define the relationships between existing organizations which do research, the relationships between the National Research Council, the Defence Research Board, the scientific secretariat, if it continues to exist, and the research which is being done and which should be done in the universities.
If this science council can do that, Mr. Chairman, then it will make a contribution; but I am sceptical about the ability of a new organization to overcome the established practices and desires of the existing agencies such as the National Research Council and the Defence Research Board. I doubt whether it will be able to make them give up any of their power, their prestige and their ability to control what is done not only by themselves but by others, and I shall go into that in some detail in a few minutes.
But even if it could do that-and this is not the time to discuss it in detail although I can tell the minister some of us will be discussing it in great detail, possibly extending over days and weeks when the estimates come before the appropriate committee

unless there is a major and revolutionary change in the thinking, in the concept of Canadian governments, federal and provincial, about the need for a tremendously expanded effort which will mean tripling and quadrupling the amount of money spent for scientific research, this country will be left far behind most of the other countries of the world.
It is easy to make the kind of speech which the minister made in vague generalities, but when we come to examine actual cases we can see how far we depart from what the minister spoke of yesterday. Some weeks ago in his capacity as a member of parliament from Montreal the minister, together with the Minister without Portfolio, sent a telegram to the government of Quebec urging it to reconsider the grants it was giving to McGill University, the university from which the minister himself graduated.
In view of that I am surprised to find that one of the most exciting, one of the most imaginative scientific research programs ever developed in Canada, conducted by the

I disagree with this view, but one of the reasons advanced for that belief is simply that we do not have enough doctors in Canada. Mr. Chairman, I am not going to speak at any length. I think I can make what general remarks I wish to make on this resolution in a very few minutes.
In view of the minister's academic, military and parliamentary record, and in view of the fact that this house is composed of a good number of members who have been bestowed with orders, decorations and degrees, I rise in a sort of humble mood to present a few ideas in support of what I consider a worth-while resolution which I trust will result in some early government action. As I said, Mr. Chairman, I trust the house will consider my remarks somewhat in the nature of fireside musings on scientific policy on the part of a comparative simpleton in this field. I do not pretend to be an expert in this regard. I am speaking as a rancher and as a member of parliament without very much knowledge of this aspect of life. However, I have given some thought to it.
Let me say first of all that I have always aimed at viewing my life as a whole in an attempt to adopt a sort of philosophy of life. My philosophy is based on four firm beliefs. The minister may look at me and think this is a bit out of order in the consideration of a resolution such as the one before us, but I think before I am finished I will have gained some measure of support.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
First of all, I believe in the first clause of the old Westminster catechism, that the chief end of man is to glorify God and enjoy him forever with all the implications and manifestations surrounding that first doctrine. Second, I believe we should aim to teach all human beings a reverence for all living
March 18, 1966

Science Council of Canada things in creation. Third, I believe when men are dealing with public or private policy we cannot go very far wrong when we are considering a resolution like this which has as its basic purpose that we practice that old adage, waste not, want not. My fourth belief is that the Lord helps them who help themselves, and I trust that this resolution is directed to that end.
Now what in reality is the purpose of this science council? In my opinion it is to remedy the startling unevenness in our national life. I think we all agree with this opinion. We cannot measure our success as a society with the poor and underdeveloped nations. The only fair comparison must be that we must measure our achievements against our potentialities and capabilities.
To illustrate the very sharp contrasts which exist side by side in Canadian life, and which I trust this resolution is directed at, we must take note of homes which are comfortable and even lavish, while the facilities for public recreation in our cities are often still primitive. We spend immense sums to air condition offices and public buildings while we continue to allocate insignificant funds to eliminate the dangerous pollution of our atmosphere. Millions of dollars are spent for advertising all conceivable and sometimes unnecessary products, while at the same time we say we cannot afford to develop the necessary parks and recreational centres in the downtown sections of our cities.
More and more of our country's unparalleled natural beauty is being destroyed by thoughtless and unplanned exploitation. As an example of this let me refer to these terrible places where they dump all the used automobiles, which you find outside our cities and many of our towns. Millions of dollars are spent on pleasure craft in this country. This has come to be a status symbol. I have not been worried about status because within thirty days of your death most people have forgotten you, except your relatives and close friends. We cannot in many instances find unpolluted water where we can enjoy swimming and the other water sports. Canadians have developed a great capacity for solving mechanical problems and creating technical wonders, while at the same time we tolerate great areas of shabbiness and ugliness in our cities and our countryside which debase our lives and our culture.
I trust this resolution will provide an opportunity for the logical and moral development of our physical resources. Under the 
present circumstances I may say, in terms of ill health and unemployment, there is continued misuse of our human resources. This misuse is inexcusable, and I trust that under this resolution an attempt will be made to solve this waste of human resources. Let us face it. In the midst of progress and plenty for the majority we find that many live their lives in despair because they are shackled by generations of disadvantages imposed by society and by the lack of opportunity surrounding them.
Now tremendous possibilities for the application of science can be found if this resolution is acted upon in national planning for the prevention of disease, training of doctors and the provision of the physical plants in which work can be undertaken or the healing of human beings.
Now just briefly, according to figures I have received we are spending about 75 cents per capita for medical research, whereas by comparison in the United States a single agency, the National Institute of Health, spent about $5.35 per capita last year. I think this explains what can be done in this country to improve the situation with respect to the development of hospitals, medicare plans and national health. The application of science in the development of national and provincial policies, for the conservation of land, water, forests and wildlife, offers tremendous possibilities and great opportunities to this council.
However, for policies to be effective they must be understood. This requires a sound campaign of education on the part of the federal, provincial and municipal governments and organizational interest in giving effect to the policy expressed in this resolution. This legislation is a vehicle through which a national policy for the utilization of scientific methods can be provided for the development of the individual and the nation. The government has to take action to make certain of this fact.
Research into all aspects of human endeavour relating to the conservation and development of our human and natural resources is urgently required, as well as the co-ordination of that research and activity. All types of organizations in Canada are urging research in such various fields as agricultural organizations, labour organizations, organizations representing industry, various conservation groups and communities

and so on. What is required is some leadership from the federal government under the provisions of this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, in reverting to motions I want to say to the hon. gentleman who was speaking in committee that I regret to have had to interrupt him at this stage. However, I am sure he will fully understand, and I will just be taking up a few moments.
I rise to make a declaration that is being made by fourteen countries of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization at this hour. Normally the Prime Minister would be making this statement. However, he has gone to welcome the Queen Mother, who is arriving in Ottawa at this moment.
Mr. Speaker, the government of France on March 10 delivered a note to the Canadian ambassador in Paris setting out the position of that government regarding France's future participation in NATO.
The French note which I tabled this morning states that France intends to withdraw all its remaining land and air forces still remaining under NATO command. French naval forces have already been withdrawn. France also requires the removal from French territory of all NATO military headquarters, including SHAPE itself. Finally, France requires the withdrawal of foreign forces and installations from France, unless the forces are placed under French rather than NATO operational command.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)
It is the view of the Canadian government that Canadian forces at the disposition of the alliance in Europe should be under the operational command of the Supreme Allied
DEBATES	2875
Statement re French Aide Memoire Commander. The direct implication for Canada of the French decision, therefore, is that we shall have to relinquish our air base at Marville and the air division headquarters at Metz and relocate these forces and facilities elsewhere. Other Canadian forces in Europe outside of France are not directly affected.
The French government also addressed notes to all other members of NATO. These notes are all substantially similar. The notes addressed to the United States, the Federal Republic of Germany and Canada deal additionally with matters which are the subject of bilateral agreements with France.
The French intention to withdraw from the integrated military arrangements established under NATO has been the subject of consultation among the other 14 members of the organization who have determined to maintain the integrated defence structure of the alliance. The experience of the last two world wars and modern developments in warfare permit no effective alternative to unified command and planning arrangements for allied forces. Recognizing the need for continuing these proven arrangements, Canada has today joined the other members of NATO in making the following declaration:
The following declaration has been agreed between the heads of governments of Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the Federal Republic of Germany, Greece, Iceland, Italy, Luxembourg, The Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Turkey, the United Kingdom and the United States of America.
The North Atlantic Treaty and the organization established under it are both alike essential to the security of our countries.
The Atlantic alliance has ensured its efficacy as an instrument of defence and deterrence by the maintenance in peacetime of an integrated and interdependent military organization, in which, as in no previous alliance in history, the efforts and resources of each are combined for the common security of all. We are convinced that this organization is essential and will continue. No system of bilateral arrangements can be a substitute.
The North Atlantic Treaty and the organization are not merely instruments of the common defence. They meet a common political need and reflect the readiness and determination of the member countries of the North Atlantic community to consult and act together wherever possible in the safeguard of their freedom and security in the furtherance of international peace, progress and prosperity.
I would remind the house before I take my seat that the government of France in the note it has sent to Canada does not, as I said during the question period today, propose to denounce the treaty.

Mr. Speaker, the conclusion arrived at by the minister on behalf of the government of Canada will, I believe, command the support of all Canadians. There is nothing more serious than the possibility of the disintegration of an organization that has meant so much to the peace of Europe and of the world. Apparently General de Gaulle believes that the dangers of 1945, 1946, 1947 and 1948 are no longer in existence. I only wish that events which have taken place could give support to that view. We still face a terrible threat from Communist aggression, and this organization, built on unity and common safety, has done much to preserve the peace.
Let me recall the situation in the dark days of 1916 and 1917 during the first world war. When there was disunity in command there was defeat on the field of battle. It was difficult to bring the nations together at that time and it was difficult in the last war. However, it was not until unity was established that the forces of freedom were able to move forward. That unity must be preserved today.
What the declaration by the French government will mean is that we shall have to withdraw our forces from France. Supreme headquarters will be removed from Paris and our headquarters at Metz will also have to be moved.
This is an announcement that cannot but cause deep concern to all of us who believe in the necessity for an integrated command as a basis for the survival of each and all of us. There is apparently nothing that can be done to bring about any change of opinion on the part of General de Gaulle and the Republic of France. That being so, we must accept the declaration that he has made, at the same time making it clear on behalf of Canada that we believe in the continuance of NATO and that the nations of NATO shall continue to remain united.
In saying that I realize that the note states that NATO will continue, but NATO without an integrated command will be as non-existent as it is possible for that organization to be. So the remaining nations in NATO must show, with the kind of spirit that is necessary today, that they will stand together.
It is regrettable that France has taken this stand. I called it a truculent one the other day and the minister took objection to the use of the expression. It is a stand difficult to understand but it is one that we must meet

by bringing into still closer relationship the remaining nations of NATO in an integrated command, at the same time doing our part to implement those portions of the NATO agreement having to do with the strengthening of economies as between nations. Indeed, what has taken place is a challenge to open up new vistas in international relationships. One of those things which I think should be carefully considered is an Atlantic community built upon the principles of equity, and common purpose, thereby assuring that the nations which stand for freedom will stand together in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, we too regret the determination of the French to withdraw from the integrated planning and activities within NATO, though we are glad they are not withdrawing from NATO itself. It seems to us that this determination is based upon the idea of the sovereignty of individual nations, an idea which is not appropriate in these times. It is an anachronism, and we regret this step.
[DOT] (1:10 p.m.)
There is, of course, as the French aide memoire indicates, a very great diminution in the threat which existed and therefore in the need for an integrated defence within NATO. But we do not believe that the threat, although greatly diminished, has been entirely removed. We think that the French aide memoire is perfectly right in saying that the centre of international crisis has shifted from Europe to Asia and to other parts of the world. We therefore welcome the announced intention of the 14 remaining nations to continue to discuss integrated plans for dealing with that threat, diminished though it may be.
It seems to us that any alliance in the modern day is not meaningful unless it provides for close integration of action and military plans. However, Mr. Speaker, there is one aspect of this matter that has not been touched on. That is the belief we have that the French proposal to invite Canada to withdraw her air bases and other installations from French territory gives us an opportunity to do something that ought to have been done long ago, and that is to reconsider very carefully and very radically our whole strategy and our present strategic plans within NATO.
We have long expressed our disquiet about the reliance upon a tactical nuclear response within NATO. We have long expressed the view that the Canadian NATO role would
March 18, 1966	COMMONS
be far more appropriate if it consisted of a contribution to a mobile reserve. We hope that the new plans that will be made necessary by the initiative of France will include for the alliance as a whole serious reconsideration of whether the massive line-up of tactical nuclear weapons within NATO is appropriate at the present time with the diminished threat and, indeed, with the risk that this sort of strategy involves.
We therefore hope that the opportunity will be taken in all these discussions for Canada to do what we think should have been done some time ago, namely, to renegotiate her role in NATO and assume a more appropriate role in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I have a suggestion and a few brief remarks I wish to make. It is my belief that there is a place for the establishment in Canada of a Canadian college of conservation. I believe the time is ripe for the establishment of a Canadian college devoted to teaching the philosophy and principles of the conservation of renewable natural resources.
The idea first struck me when I was informed of overseas students coming to Canada. In many cases those students go on a six month tour across Canada to see Canadian industry, Canadian agriculture and Canadian development in other respects. After they have completed their tour, left this country and returned to their own countries, it seems to me they have not received any, as it were, unified instruction as to the purpose of their visit. I am suggesting to the minister that this proposed council could consider the development of a Canadian college of conservation in a very modest way in some appropriate southern part of the country, which in my
DEBATES	2877
Science Council of Canada view ought to be something like the Koote-nays where there is water, land and forest.
The buildings would be built of logs. I think there is an opportunity here for the development of artistic values. The buildings could be staffed with a small administrative skeleton staff. The college would be able to make provision say for 50 students, in the first instance, whether they be from overseas or from Canada. Provision could be made for professors who are competent in their own fields to be asked to come from the various universities across Canada to give lectures there for one or two weeks on the particular subjects in which they are competent.
I am making this suggestion because I have discussed the matter with a number of people who know about these things. I believe there is a place for this type of college in Canada. You might call it almost a technical training school. It would be a college where students would learn the principles and ideas behind the whole philosophy of conservation, not necessarily with respect to dealing with pure or applied science but so that at the end of one or two years, or whatever period was decided upon, the persons who had attended this college, whether they were from Canada or abroad, would receive a diploma, as it were, from the Canadian college of conservation which would indicate that they had been trained in these principles.
If this is done, when overseas students return to their own countries they will have obtained some knowledge of what we are aiming for in the direction conservation, and if they are Canadians, especially persons who are not particularly interested in academic life at its higher levels, they will have opportunities for employment with various organizations or various levels of government in this country where they can practice the principles they have learned at the college. I should like to see this matter explored because I think it could be undertaken at very small cost compared with the results which could be obtained. I believe that our university students and high school students must continue to be informed of the value of these proposals if we are going to maintain and improve in this country our present standard of living.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. I have enough confidence in the minister to believe that he is determined on this question. He had a good administrative record in the army, and I believe that if he

Science Council of Canada applies the same discipline to this organization, shall I say, as he has to other things we will get results. Questions were asked by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. Some of these were detailed and might better await the production of the bill before they are discussed. However, there was one general question very directly relating to the resolution itself. It was: Why should we set up a science council when we already have the National Research Council? I tried to make clear that the Glassco Commission in its report on government administration-and this view was subsequently supported by Dr. Mackenzie in his examination of the problem-had reached the conclusion that the National Research Council, which has been doing excellent work in its field and about which I shall have more to say later, has tended over the years to concern itself with two main tasks, the allocation of resources to individuals in the academic stream by way of university scholarships and bursaries and, second, the operation of large, substantial and successful laboratories under its own direct control. As a consequence of these two main preoccupations there has perhaps not been sufficient attention paid by the council to the larger question of the delineation of scientific objectives for Canada as a whole, not merely the government, not merely the academic community or the industrial community, but for all Canadians.
The making of such an analysis will, of course, be one of the principal and first tasks of the science council. A number of people have felt, and I am in agreement with this view, that this new focusing of attention on analysis and objectives could be better done by a new body set up for that particular purpose than by redirecting the National Research Council in this sense. Dr. Mackenzie, as I mentioned, supports such a view. In short, we would do better to appoint a new advisory body and this advisory body should not be made in any way subordinate to the National Research Council, given the nature of the people we hope to appoint to it and their stature in the community. The new council will have an existence altogether independent of the National Research Council.

Mr. Chairman, this is a bill which will be desirable in the light of the enactment of the bill which has just been read a first time, namely, the bill to establish the Science Council of Canada. I should like to take this occasion to point out to hon. members that this year the National Research Council, which everyone will agree has had quite an outstanding record in its dedication to the support of excellence will be celebrating its 50th anniversary.
The council started in 1916 as a body to establish scholarships for graduate students and to provide grants in aid of research for professors. It was only some nine years later that the National Research Council organized laboratories and began the kind of work for which it has since become so well known. In world war II the council was successful in mobilizing all the scientific and technological agencies in Canada and out of this arose such wartime developments as radar, atomic energy, and scientific backing for our military and economic leaders in the military and civilian fields during the war.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
The National Research Council during the war set up Research Enterprises Limited, a manufacturing concern for the rapid production of gun sights and about $300 million worth of radar equipment designed by the National Research Council. Following the war the National Research Council continued to expand not only its ideas but its activities and from this fabric was created two agencies which in themselves, in an independent way, have achieved very considerable success in the scientific world and considerable renown. The first of these, of course, was the Defence Research Board which was created in 1947, and subsequently Atomic Energy of Canada Limited in 1952.

The aim of seeking new frontiers of knowledge on the part of the National Research Council has been reinforced by a very important service to the Canadian scientific community under the name of the N.R.C. technical information service. This technical information service does provide scientific information across Canada and abroad but principally to Canadians and is, I might point out, very extensively used. Inquiries answered by the technical information service amount to some 17,000 a year.
The resolution has for its purpose support for a bill to amend the National Research Council Act. The National Research Council has in its present form two official titles. One is The Honorary Advisory Council for Scientific and Industrial Research and the other is the more commonly used title, National Research Council. Since the second title receives more general use throughout the world and the words "of Canada" usually are added thereto to distinguish it from the national research councils of other countries, it is proposed to abandon the formal and little used title and to add the words "of Canada" to the second title, making it read in English, National Research Council of Canada, and in French, Conseil National de Recherches du Canada.
Since the proposed Science Council of Canada is to have the duty of advising the government on scientific policy, the Research Council Act should be amended to relieve the Research Council of this duty.
It is proposed to take advantage of this opportunity to make some minor amendments to eliminate anomalies which have become apparent in the operation of the council, and to introduce certain desirable improvements. I think, Mr. Chairman, with those remarks we might be able to concur in the resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, because of the unavoidable absence of the Minister of Forestry, who is detained at home on account of illness, I have been asked to introduce this resolution.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
The purpose of the resolution now before us is to establish a special fund for rural economic development. As hon. members know, the ARDA rural development program in co-ordination with other programs is tackling the problems of rural low income throughout the rural areas of Canada. However, as hon. members will also know from their own studies, rural low income, poverty and underdevelopment are particularly deep-seated in certain rural problem areas in Canada.
As the ARDA program has evolved, it has become evident that special comprehensive and co-ordinated development programs for these areas are required if living standards for the people in these areas are to be greatly improved in a reasonable length of time.
This approach, which might be described as a specific regional development approach for these areas, involves the following process: First, the selection of these areas which are subject to widespread low income, have major adjustment and development problems and have recognized development potential.
Second, the undertaking of physical, economic and social studies and investigations to determine the development problems and potentials of the areas.
Third, the involvement of local people through the preparation of comprehensive rural development plans.
Fourth, the undertaking of a broad range of projects for the implementation of the plan, with the objective of increasing income and raising standards of living in the area.
Planning in several of these areas has now reached the point where rural development comprehensive plans, including proposals for specific projects, are being prepared and it is obvious that special provisions will be required to finance the development plans. The areas where the process is at this stage include the Interlake area in Manitoba, the lower St. Lawrence in the Gaspe area of 
Quebec, and northeastern New Brunswick. A number of areas in other provinces also are proceeding with the development of plans.
A bill to provide for the economic and social development of these areas is being proposed in order to provide special financial assistance beyond that normally available under the cost-sharing provisions of the ARDA program to implement these plans. I believe this bill provides an important forward step in the most comprehensive program which is now being developed to meet the particular problems of certain rural areas in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief comments regarding this resolution. They will take the form of questions which have been in my mind and which I think have been in the minds of other hon. members. I am reminded that this resolution is probably the beginning of great changes in our rural areas and I wonder whether they will be changes for the better. I note that the resolution highlights the word "comprehensive" in the fifth line thereof. I cannot comprehend what the goal of the government is when I hear that the legislation will authorize-I suppose we will come to this point later-that farms be bought and grouped into larger economically paying units, and then sold back to the farmers. I cannot see any glowing future for the Canadian rural economy in the method which I understand the government is contemplating. I know that larger units are inevitable under present mechanized methods of agriculture.
Why not let the farmers undertake this development themselves? Who knows what type of unit a certain large block of land will be turned into by the government and its bureaucratic organizations? The new unit will comprise smaller farms of say 50 to 100 acres fenced into one area which the government will then call an economic unit. It may not be an economic unit for prospective buyers of that large new block of land. Anyone interested in acquiring one of these so-called
March 18, 1966

economic units might not use it for a purpose which would result in the government calling it an economic unit at all.
I am sure hon. members will get the point I am trying to make. It is that we should let the farmers, through their own private enterprise, buy up these blocks of land themselves and turn them into whatever type of unit individual farmers and their families find best for their future. I am sure these blocks of land would end up with a much more economical and easier to handle mortgage, one of which could be amortized well within their lifetime, instead of the farmers becoming mortgaged to the government for large sums of money which are sure to be entailed in the plan I understand the government is contemplating.
I am also concerned about other facets, Mr. Chairman. If in a rural area smaller farms are purchased to be combined into larger units, the occupants of the original holdings would be forced to move. There still exist today 50 acre and 100 acre blocks. My family has a farm of 125 acres in Richmond township which has been in our family now for three generations. This is the type of holding I have in mind. I am referring to quite productive areas of that kind. If three farms of that size were put into one holding, a holding that is much more adaptable to this age of automation and the economy of the day, the occupants of the original holdings could only move away to urban areas. But, Mr. Chairman, to what benefit? These people who will be displaced are at present making perhaps a meagre living but at least they are living on the farms. They will be cast on to a cruel and competitive labour market which is strange to them and will earn wages which will still be insufficient to enable them to cope with the highly inflated cost of living currently confronting our economy. In other words, these people can live just as well and much cheaper in their natural rural environment.
I claim that the government would do better to work diligently and steadily to remedy the present high cost of living which is a bugbear and an obstacle to the people engaged in agriculture in our rural areas as well as to people in urban areas of limited means.
These are some of the questions I have in mind, Mr. Chairman. I also agree with the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale when he asks how far $50 million will go. It will not go very far, as he said, when spread
Rural Development Act over ten provinces. I am sure other hon. members will discuss these questions when we get past the resolution stage and into the readings of the bill, and I hope that the government in their rural development plan will govern themselves accordingly.
I might also ask what the government proposes to do to improve other good economic facets which already exist, especially in the province of Ontario. Hydro is available all through the province in almost every rural locality. The little red schoolhouse has now gone and modern schools have been built or are being built. There are good roads into almost every rural area. What can the federal government do to improve the economic and social status of rural areas in Ontario? I just point out these things, Mr. Chairman, and I look forward to sound discussion in the later stages of this measure.

The Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, passed in 1961, provides authority for the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces for the sharing of costs in connection with three types of undertakings in rural areas: First, those for the efficient use and economic development of submarginal agricultural lands; second, projects designed to develop income and employment opportunities and improve standards of living in rural agricultural areas; third, projects to develop and conserve water supplies for agricultural purposes and improve soil conditions for agricultural efficiency.
Since the launching of the program in 1962 effective program approaches have been jointly developed with the provinces to meet the adjustment needs in the rural agricultural areas of Canada. I am sure hon. members would be interested to know that so far $80 million has been committed for such programs and that all provinces have participated in them. I want to clarify remarks which were made during the introduction of the previous resolution and point out again that the amount of $50 million which was mentioned is over and above the funds made available under the regular ARDA program.
Studies undertaken under this program have indicated the widespread nature of rural low income. In fact, in 1961 almost 500,000 rural families had an income of less than $3,000 per year. A significant proportion of these families reside in areas in the Atlantic provinces and along the fringes of settlement throughout the rest of Canada where, strictly speaking, they cannot be said to live in rural agricultural areas. It is now obvious that the rural development program approaches which have been developed can be extended to meet the adjustment and rehabilitation needs of these rural people who are outside the agricultural sector. Through the proposed amendments to the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, the effective program approaches which can be devised under the present act may be made available to the outport fishing settlements of Newfoundland, to the isolated rural settlements of northern Quebec and Ontario, the native population of the northern fringe areas of the prairie provinces and to the scattered areas of rural population in British Columbia.

Further proposed amendments to the Act provide for a change in the short title to "Rural Development Act" and provide authority for the payment of remuneration to members of the advisory committees.
These committees would be altogether different from the ones mentioned in the previous resolution. These were supposed to be committees formed to advise the federal government when definite proposals are received from the provinces. In this case the reference is to local committees that will be established within the province or within certain areas or municipalities in order to formulate programs to be presented to the provinces.
