The association agrees with the feeling that the present air traffic control situation is a potentially dangerous one in relation to air safety. Normal recruiting through the Civil Service Commission is much too long, and the training period required is such that only emergency action taken immediately can solve this problem.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity of bringing this condition to the attention of the minister, in this instance the Minister without Portfolio, in the hope that in line with the legislation which we are discussing, he will pass it on to the Minister of Transport. I urge that this situation, not only in the Montreal airport but in others which I am told are affected, be looked into speedily.

Mr. Chairman, I realize that the terms of this resolution and the bill to follow appear to deal primarily with the functions of the Air Transport Board in so far as accidents and safety are concerned. However, Mr. Chairman, there is a reference here to increasing from three to five the size of the Air Transport Board. I believe he also said there were new procedures for appeals to the minister from the decisions of the board. The resolution also points out that these appointments shall now be for a period not exceeding ten years. I hope the Minister without Portfolio will not consider me out of order if I suggest to him that it is about time something was done with respect to the Air Transport Board, because there have been some rather sad experiences in the Prairies with regard to the consequences of certain decisions which have been made by the board.

March 18, 1966
Aeronautics Act
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Chairman, having said that, I must hasten to add that I am not criticizing the Air Transport Board by itself or suggesting that there was any prior knowledge of some of these mistakes which I think have been made. However, it appears that there were some mistakes and it also appears that there was some kind of a deal, if I may call it that, between TransAir and Trans-Canada Air Lines which was not brought to the attention of the Air Transport Board hearings. I am talking about the application of TransAir to provide services from Winnipeg to Brandon, Yorkton, Regina, Swift Current, Medicine Hat and Calgary. There was never any indication before the Air Transport Board hearings that Trans-Canada Air Lines was going to give or transfer $500,000 worth of equipment to the line that was successful in taking over the service from Trans-Canada at the time. Yet, Mr. Chairman, that is exactly what happened after the decision was handed down.
We complained when this happened, Mr. Chairman. Time after time we complained that something was wrong, that something was unfair about the fact that all these assets were given by Trans-Canada Air Lines, as it was then, to TransAir after Trans-Canada Air Lines had been relieved of providing the service and TransAir had been given the francise or the right to provide the service by the Air Transport Board ruling.
Had any of the other air carriers known that they would receive two DC-3 aircraft, I believe it was, one Viscount aircraft and all the other equipment necessary to service these aircraft, communications facilities, and so on, then there would have been an altogether different kind of application made for this so-called milk run or southern prairie service. What hurts even more, Mr. Chairman, is that after TransAir received all this equipment it provided this service for only 11 months and then withdrew.
The reason I bring this matter up again is that TransAir are apparently going to withdraw from some more services they undertook to provide on the prairies. Yet I do not see any action on the part of the Minister of Transport, or by Air Canada for that matter, to recover some of the $500,000 worth of equipment which was given to TransAir. This is why I should like the Minister without Portfolio to know that a lot of people on the prairies are greatly disturbed about the withdrawal of all their regional air services. They

are disturbed that a company which has been given what is, in effect, an enormous grant at public expense in the form of aircraft and parts is withdrawing from services it should be providing, leaving them with nothing.
During the course of Board of Transport Commissioners hearings, and in hearings before the Committee on Transport and Communications, we are told day after day by C.P.R. witnesses that the reason the C.P.R. is withdrawing from railway passenger services is that the air lines are taking over the business of transporting passengers from one city to another. Yet it seems all these cities in western Canada are also having their air line services withdrawn, particularly those provided by TransAir.
When TransAir and several other companies attended the hearings before the Air Transport Board, I am not sure of the date but I believe in late 1962 or 1963, they undertook to provide a service and were granted the franchise for particular routes. Some of the people on the prairies believe that they never really gave those services a chance to succeed. While some of the other applicants may have been successful, though it is difficult to know because they never had the opportunity, we do not believe that TransAir gave the service a chance to succeed.
Looking at this in retrospect, I should like the minister to know that we do not like the fact that these assets were handed over to TransAir, who then withdrew their services. These old DC-3 aircraft and the equipment necessary in the provision of ground services, and so on, may not be too important, and perhaps they were not too valuable. But included in the subsidies or gifts, or whatever you want to call them, was a Viscount aircraft which we are told is worth about $350,000. Why that was included we cannot understand, because the aircraft was not even used on that route. What is so difficult to understand, Mr. Chairman, is that there was never any indication that Trans-Canada Air Lines was going to give TransAir that equipment until after the decision of the Air Transport Board had been rendered.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to criticize the Air Transport Board, because perhaps they did not know about this equipment either. But T.C.A. was, and still is, a publicly owned corporation, and any time they give away $500,000 worth of equipment I think it is the business of this parliament to look into the matter.
March 18, 1966

When we asked the Minister of Transport questions about this matter, as far as I am concerned we did not get any satisfactory answers. The minister said he would ask the president of Air Canada, as it is now, about it, but to my knowledge there has never been a satisfactory explanation given to this house, in spite of all the representations which were made, as to why and under what circumstances this $500,000 worth of equipment was given to TransAir. That company has now withdrawn services from all of the routes it undertook to provide, I believe with the exception of one, which is Regina-Sas-katoon-Prince Albert. All the other routes in the southern prairie regional air service have now been discontinued.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to labour this point greatly. Several months ago when we were much exercised about it we raised the question with the Minister of Transport but were not given any satisfactory explanation. We still expect an explanation, and this matter becomes even more important in view of TransAir having made further applications to withdraw other routes within the last few days.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister who introduced this resolution to amend the Aeronautics Act whether the words in the second and third lines of the resolution "to prescribe charges for the use of facilities and services provided by the Minister of Transport" refer to such things as the fees collected for these monopolistic taxicab and limousine services at airports like Mal-ton, Dorval, and other Canadian airports, and fees collected through the monopolistic parking arrangements which are made. I shall not proceed further on this matter if I receive a favourable reply, but I do have a third item which I should like to take up.
No, Mr. Chairman, this act makes no provision for or reference to what the hon. member is talking about. It applies merely to services rendered to aircraft in flight.

Mr. Chairman, I think you will have to agree with me that the wording of the resolution could be interpreted to read "charges for the use of facilities provided by the Minister of Transport". Certainly facilities are provided by the Minister of Transport at various airports for taxicab service or limousine service-as they call it, to get around the law-and for parking facilities.
Aeronautics Act
I have a third point I wish to make, but before I do so I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Medicine Hat upon the comments he made on the resolution.
This resolution will provide, among other things, that the Air Transport Board shall consist of not less than three and not more than five members. I should like to be able to stand up in this house and congratulate the Minister of Transport-and I am referring to the Minister of Transport now, not to the Minister without Portfolio-on finally having realized the proper way to bring in these changes which are so necessary. I say that because I have in my hand Hansard for April last year, when quite a few members of the house, including myself, were discussing at some length supplemental estimates. It is very nice to have the proper procedure followed on this resolution, which is to provide that the Air Transport Board shall consist of not less than three and not more than five members.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I hold in my hand supplementary estimates E and at page 29 we have an item that was withdrawn after opposition from all parts of the house, because we were opposed to legislation by supplemental estimates. The item under vote 75d reads:
Vote 75d-Salaries and Other Expenses-To extend the purposes of Transport Vote 75 to the Main Estimates, 1964-65 to authorize the Governor in Council notwithstanding section 7 of the Aeronautics Act, to appoint two members of the Air Transport Board in addition to the number provided for by that Act, such members to hold office during pleasure for a term not exceeding three years and to be paid such salary as may be fixed by the Governor in Council, $1.
I draw to the attention of the house the fact that the proper type of legislation is now being introduced. I sincerely hope that since it is proper, it will pass. I do believe that we are entitled to comment on the manner in which this was first brought down as a supplementary estimate in March of 1965, and what was done at that time by people who are opposed to this type of legislation.
When I stated that I could congratulate the Minister of Transport for having brought in the bill properly, I am not unaware of the fact that during the past three weeks we have been forced to rush through supplementary estimates without any consideration being given to the great bulk of them. We were told that if we were to discuss at length the estimates for the year ending March 31, 1966, we would be holding up the legislation of the

March 18. 1966
Aeronautics Act
country, the civil service could not be paid, and we must not hold them up. Supplementary estimates for the items of $1 went through at a rate that can only be decried as unseemly by people who believe that things should be done in order.
Bill No. C-140, for the House of Commons of Canada, which was passed in the last three weeks has 18 $1 items, practically every one of which is legislation by supplementary estimates.
That was a proper bill, coming under a proper resolution. Now, as I refer to item No. 9 I can hardly congratulate the government for doing the proper thing, as compared with legislation by supplementary estimates one year ago, when within the last three weeks they have put through 18 items of legislation under the $1 supplementary estimates.
Under the Department of Transport, in Bill C-140, item 8b reads:
To authorize in accordance with such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may prescribe, the transfer of the assets and administration of the Pension Fund of the British Columbia Pilotage District established under the Canada shipping Act, 1934,-[DOT]
And so on.
-$1.
This is brand new legislation, and it is under the Department of Transport, under supplementary estimates of $1.
Then I refer to the Department of Transport, air services. There is an item passed under supplementary estimates. This is legislation by supplementary estimates. 1 do not like it and I believe the great majority of the members of the House of Commons do not like it.
Vote 35b reads:
Construction or Acquisition of Buildings, Works, Land and Equipment including national airports (as determined by the Minister of Transport.) and related facilities, including authority, notwithstanding section 30, of the Financial Administration Act, to increase to $16,216,500 the commitments for the current fiscal year for Radio Aids to Air and Marine Navigation-$1.
Still, under the Department of Transport, vote 83b reads:	.
Notwithstanding any limitation that may be contained in section 265 of the Railway Act, to authorize the payment of an amount not exceeding $2 million from The Railway Grade Crossing Fund to be applied towards the cost of any relocation of the Canadian Pacific Railway line in Sault Ste. Marie pursuant to an Order of the Board-$1.

I have only read you three items where you have legislation by supplementary estimates of the Department of Transport. Exactly the same thing has been done in the last three weeks that was blocked one year ago. If what we did in the last three weeks is perfectly in order and something which we should all admire, why did they bring in the new resolution under item No. 9 relating to the Aeronautics Act? I submit that this resolution now being introduced is proper and is right, and should be passed. I would point out at the same time that while the Minister of Justice is doing one thing correctly with his left hand, I have just quoted Department of Transport supplementary estimates showing things are being done wrongly with the right hand.
I believed the lesson that we endeavoured to teach one year ago could have been learned permanently. In the case of supplementary estimates one year ago vote 75d which was withdrawn and now appears properly as a resolution, will be properly included in the bill.
I have to make these comments because I do not like legislation by supplementary estimates. I have said that for the past several years, and I will continue to say so as long as I am a member of this house. By one of these supplementary estimates of $1, there is brought about an alteration in the terms of an international treaty relating to fish, and to the Great Lakes. This is done by means of a $1 supplementary estimate.
I raise this objection in the same manner in which the hon. member for Medicine Hat raised his.

I should like to add a few words to what was said by the hon. member for Pictou. Before I do so I must say that I was rather intrigued by the hon. member for York-Humber this afternoon. I am not too sure that he fully understands the principle of $1 votes. I am surprised that somebody on the government side did not raise the question that the hon. member was casting a reflection on a decision of the house, and therefore that he was off base in that. However, he did not carry on for too long a time; therefore that point was not raised.
The appropriate bill that was passed and the decisions taken by this house, according to the rules of the house, are not subject to criticism in the way put forward by the hon. member. However I will agree with some of the things the hon. member said, although I
March 18. 1966

think that if he had realized what is being done by the proposed legislation he might have had second thoughts.
The hon. member suggests by his remark that last year the request to appoint an additional two members to the Air Transport Board by way of a supplementary estimate was legislation by the back door. That measure may have been necessary because it was wanted at that time. It would not have affected the possible composition of the board. Now, with the changing of the board, since the legislation has been passed, those people who are in office may be through, and the minister and the government need not reappoint the members who are in. This is the neatest way of putting the guillotine to any surviving board members. I am not suggesting that that may happen; but it could happen. Under the aegis of this particular minister, I am sure if they are not of the proper political stripe they can pack their bags.
I can tell the hon. member that amending the act and creating a board under a slightly different name, or under a different section, puts an end to the old board. That is what they did with the Economic Council of Canada. The National Productivity Council was killed off simply by changing its name.
In addition to this, Mr. Chairman, I want clarification from the minister piloting the bill. It is not disclosed in the resolution, but did he not also say that the act would provide for appeal from the Transport Board to the minister? Am I not correct in that?
Yes.

My worst fears are confirmed. If a decision of the Air Transport Board is subject to an appeal to the minister, the board then becomes a direct instrument of government policy, because the board members will first clear with the minister as to what the board's decision must be. Under no circumstances should there be an appeal to a minister from a board. Certainly if it is the intention to appeal to the minister, that is abominable. We do not make the Income Tax Appeal Board responsible to the Minister of National Revenue. We do not allow that an appeal shall lie to the Minister of National Revenue. No other boards that I recall may have their decisions referred to an appeal before the minister.
Let us create some other body; or, for that matter, let an appeal go to the Exchequer 23033-1831
Aeronautics Act
Court. But an appeal from the decision of the Air Transport Board to the minister is abominable. We have something new in that concept.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he not aware that the Railway Act provides for appeal from the judgments of the Board of Transport Commissioners to the Governor in Council?

Yes, and I say this: the Governor in Council is not the minister. I think it has been salutory in many instances that provision has been made for an appeal to the Governor in Council. But in this particular instance the provision for appeal makes the board an instrument of government policy, or part of the executive, and this I think is wrong.
Instead of some of the other matters which the minister brought forward I should like to have heard a declaration from the government with respect to a regional air carrier policy, something for which the hon. member for Medicine Hat has been pressing. I recall this was to have been one of the great pronouncements during the 60 days of decision. This was to have been a source of pride and joy.
Certainly, when the former member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) sat on this side of the house, two weeks could not go by but he was asking: When is there to be a regional air transport policy? Shortly afterwards, he and his friends took over-and they have been deciding ever since. The result has been the sort of morass which the hon. member for Medicine Hat has indicated. I know carriers who are waiting to determine whether to buy this or that type of aircraft; they have to wait until the government reaches a conclusion as to what the regional air carrier policy is to be.
In the interval, who suffers? The public. As far as TransAir is concerned, this looked like a tidy deal. I know that Pacific Western and Northwest Industries made applications for a part of this franchise at least, and were turned down. But we know that the former president of TransAir was a good friend of the present administration. I do not know what the arrangements with the company are now, but certainly the net result has been

March 18, 1966
Aeronautics Act
that there is uncertainty with regard to passenger transport on the prairies in the secondary centres. Carriers who would like to double their fleets and who have an opportunity to buy aircraft, cannot do so.
Has no one tried an aerial bus service on regional air routes? We have one between Edmonton and Calgary and it is highly effective. 1 will admit there is a high concentration of passengers. Maybe the Department of Transport does not like this bus service because it does not use Department of Transport airports. Maybe the department would like to force this traffic to the international airport at Edmonton. But the passenger service started initially in 1963 using DC-8s and less. The company has now gone through DC-6Bs and is now moving into Electras. There is every indication that this type of service would be well patronized. It is not supplied for week end travel, but that is all right; I am sure that a number of these secondary places on the prairies would be satisfied if they had regional service five days a week. Certainly it would be better than nothing.
I am not entirely sanguine about the amendments which have been proposed. Some of them may be in order. It is inconsequential to suggest that we must amend the act so that the Minister of Transport may charge $1 or $1.25 for lunch when passengers are using a Department of Transport plane. This is a question which the Auditor General raised a few years ago, and it is one of the amendments. There is nothing very serious about that.
However, the other matters, the provision of the right of appeal from the Air Transport Board to the minister, this change in the personnel of the board, appointments to run for ten years, are of more substance. I note that the retirement age is the age of 70. Why, I do not know. In the case of the Supreme Court the age is 75. In the case of other boards, it is 65. Someone will have to explain why that age 70 was chosen. It is one of the magical years, I suppose. In any event we shall be interested in seeing the bill when it comes down. We shall also be interested in having the minister here.
Today we are putting through a good deal of legislation by substitution; there is a bare complement of ministers on which to operate the house. Some of these questions may be skipped over but we do not intend to let this happen when second reading comes along.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
I will try to answer it.

I should like to ask the hon. member for Edmonton West if he has read the comment of his former cabinet colleague who sits in the other place as recorded in Senate debates for March 9 on pages 286 and 287, in which the hon. Senator reflects the opinions I expressed a year ago, which are those I expressed just now with regard to legislation by supplementary estimate.
I do not know to which hon. Senator the hon. member is referring. Again, if I may refer to the rules, I am not at all sure whether it is proper to refer to this year's proceedings in the other place.

I have some comments to make on that part of the resolution which relates to an increase in size of the Air Transport Board. I did not realize until it was mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton West that the effect of this legislation would be to give the government an opportunity completely to re-open the question of the board's composition. Should this be the case I imagine that some of the present members would be re-appointed. But this does provide for an increase of five members.
Lately a number of ex-politicians have been appointed to various government boards. I do not want to be personal; some of these people are friends of mine and I think a case can be made for looking after expoliticians. Nevertheless I believe there are certain types of government boards to which appointments ought to be made on the basis of technical and professional competence. I wish to express the hope that additional appointments to the Air Transport Board will be of this type and that the vacancies will not be used merely to find a resting place for candidates who have been defeated in elections.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Another point on which I should like to comment briefly arises from that part of the resolution which deals with inquiries into aircraft accidents. This is an important subject. Unfortunately there have been a good many accidents lately and these have received a great deal of publicity. I should like to emphasize the remarks of my hon. friend from New Westminster on the subject of the prevention of accidents. This whole question
March 18. 1966



of air traffic control, including the adequacy of the control staff, is one of great importance. It becomes more important all the time as the major airports of this country are handling more and more air movements. It becomes more important as the aircraft themselves become bigger and faster, and carry more passengers.
I have had some discussions with people who work in this field. I am not satisfied that at our major airports we have sufficient people working at air traffic control to allow them to work on a regular schedule without working overtime a great deal. This is very demanding, nerve wracking work, and I want to emphasize that the question of staffing air traffic control centres is of the utmost importance and we should do more than we are doing at present to help prevent air accidents.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to make one or two brief comments on points that have been raised. I have noted what the hon. member for Pictou has said on the question of an air safety control program. The hon. member for Medicine Hat raised a question which I think we can develop elsewhere at more length about the regional air policy and the problem of TransAir at some of the western points between Winnipeg and Saskatoon.
The Air Transport Board has notified all the communities and other enterprises concerned that they have until April 1 to present material to the board by way of objection to the proposed application of TransAir to withdraw from the service. I understand date and place have not been set for that hearing, but it will probably be in Regina. The points the hon. member raised about the transfer of equipment will be mentioned to Air Canada, and I am sure raised before the board. In any event the Air Transport Board will be apprised of the debate this afternoon.
There were two or three points raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West which I deem it advisable to reply to at this stage, even though he will have an opportunity on second reading of the bill to go into them further. It is my understanding that the Aeronautics Act has always had in it a provision for appeal to the minister, and that this provision is not new. What it does in this case is to extend the right of appeal to third parties as well as to applicants. That is the only novel feature in that respect.
I am also advised that this legislation will not remove the present members from the Air Transport Board. The reason for the
Bills of Exchange Act
increase is to accommodate the increased business the board has, because of the increase in air traffic, and the increased responsibilities the board will have, especially with respect to accident investigation, if parliament approves this legislation.
Finally, we have taken note of the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, and I agree with him that the standard of appointments is an important essential which must be taken into consideration. In conclusion, I wish to thank the hon. member for St. John's East for having presided over this stage of our committee proceedings.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Turner thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-153, to amend the Aeronautics Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: PAYMENTS OF CHEQUES ON NONJURIDICAL DAYS

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (for the Minisier of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PAYMENTS OF CHEQUES ON NONJURIDICAL DAYS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. S-14, to amend the Bills of Exchange Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Chretien (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PAYMENTS OF CHEQUES ON NONJURIDICAL DAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendments to the act that are proposed in this bill are, I think, well explained in the notes, but in view of their importance to the business community perhaps I might make a few remarks.
The first amendment would enable a cheque to be presented and paid on a Saturday or on a non-juridical day, if the drawee branch is open for business, and further would enable the drawee, where applicable, to return as dishonoured a cheque presented on such a day. The purpose of the amendment is to permit the bank if it wishes to remain open on a Saturday or on a non-juridical day to conform with the business custom in a community, to follow the same practice with cheques that are presented as it would on any other business day on which it is open.
The second amendment would provide that where the bank closes on what otherwise would be a business day to give a holiday to its employees in compliance with section 26 of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, where applicable to banks, all matters relating to bills or notes are deferred to the next business day. This amendment would also

March 18. 1966
Bills of Exchange Act
permit a bank to adjust its business days to fit the custom of a community. For example, a branch might close on a Monday and remain open on a Saturday, if that was the local business custom.
This bill would also remove Easter Monday from the list of non-juridical days. It is not a general holiday under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code or in the business community generally today. For many years the observance of a holiday on Easter Monday has created an awkward situation for the bank staffs, as, rather than close for four consecutive days, it has been considered necessary to open on the Saturday following Good Friday, notwithstanding that it is not regarded as a business day under the act.
It is also proposed to remove from the act the provisions that required, in the province of Quebec only, that if a bill of exchange is dishonoured it must be protested in order to have recourse against the drawer or endorsers. With this change the practice will be the same in all provinces.
This amendment was suggested by a learned counsel from Quebec and has received the approval of the Premier of Quebec, the Executive Committee of the Chamber of Notaries, whose members are now required to prepare and serve the protest documents, and has also been approved by the banks.
Because of the importance of this bill in the business life of the country it is the intention, following the debate on second reading, to refer the bill to the house Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic affairs for study and further explanations if required.

subtopic: PAYMENTS OF CHEQUES ON NONJURIDICAL DAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, frankly, can be categorized as a form of clean-up bill following passage of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code and is an indication of what we may have to do in a number of areas as the result of the passage of that act, although I must say this is going to be a difficult proposition.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
It also indicates, by reason of a rather doctrinaire approach by the former minister of labour and the administration with regard to certain aspects of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, that we are going to affect vitally legal rights of citizens, as under the Bills of Exchange Act, and I will come to the point of how this comes about. In banking circles, under this act, there is going to be introduced an element of uncertainty, since

there is a provision for the conducting of business by the banks according to the customs of the community. In addition there is a provision to enable the banks to close on what would ordinarily be a business day. Does this mean that banks will carry this out uniformly? Are we going to get another day of the week during which banks are going to be closed?
Almost 30 years ago I went to work for one of the chartered banks. We worked on Saturdays in those days. I know the present act was amended in 1951 as a consequence of the five-day week. Now we are going to have an amendment, as a result of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, which will permit the banks to close on the days of choice by the banks. However, the banks are involved with their clients, with their customers, and the customers are involved one with another, with resulting legal obligations.
How are you going to spell out the days of grace on a bill so that you can determine precisely what are the legal rights? When are bills going to be presentable for honour, if in a local community it has been decided to follow the customs of business and you cannot predict ahead of time what they are going to do? These are some of the consequences we must consider in respect of the amendments as proposed. In addition, of course, the first amendment is a complete reversal of the law since 1951. For some reason or other in 1951, when the act was amended to do away with banking hours on Saturdays, except when the banks have been closed on a subsequent Monday or on the previous Friday, you could get away with presenting a dishonoured bill; there was no legal obligation which flowed from it. But now, after 15 years, it has been decided to reverse that completely and return to the law as it stood; that is, that if a bill was presented for payment at any time that a bank was open for business and it was dishonoured, certain legal consequences ensued. Why this was done in 1951 to somehow give us a chance to bounce a cheque or to bounce a note on Saturday morning, I do not know; but such was the case.
Now it is proposed to return to the law as it stood prior to 1951. I do say, with the application of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the banks must have the opportunity to close in order to conform with that act; it is not in respect of the scale of pay requirement under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, but rather the hours of work. Here again we have the doctrinaire approach of the farmer
March 18, 1966

minister of labour who obviously never worked in a bank. I am going to ask him right now, what do you do if there are errors and one has to balance off? There is only one thing you can do, and that is work until you have found your errors. But under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code one may have to call in somebody else who has never worked on the books, again because I have made errors today and worked tonight to clean them up, you have to give me a holiday tomorrow. If I were in a bank, I could get an extra day by making a mess of my books and having to stay late; they would have to let me off on another day.
This is one example of results of the doctrinaire approach. Others apply in the transportation and oil industry, where the whole act is riddled with illogicalities and impraticalities. We are seeing one of them now; it is a minor one, but it is there. Go to a rural branch out in the Prairies in the autumn months when there is a heavy volume of business. I can tell you it was my personal experience as a teller to have to put in long hours on busy days because of the volume of business. Are we going to quit because the Canada Labour (Standards) Code says we have to work only so many hours? Of course you don't. Here we have the same doctrinaire approach with regard to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, and it is impracticable.
Now, there are other amendments which have to do with holidays; I am not going to go into them in detail. However, in looking at the act as it stood before I must say it indicated that one of the days on which there could be a bank holiday was any day appointed by proclamation for a public holiday or for a general fast, or a general thanksgiving throughout Canada. I guess perhaps fasting is out of style today-that is for religious purposes-so we now are going to get a day of general prayer or mourning; then it says a general thanksgiving throughout Canada.

Commercial Fisheries Act in order to determine what participation the federal government could take in the development of the inland fisheries.
Reference was also made at the resolution stage to the participation of the province of British Columbia in these matters. Reference has also been made at the resolution stage of this bill to the possibility of training fishermen for the deep sea fishery. In recent months there has been an unprecedented demand for such fishermen. During the last 10 or 12 months we could see that such a demand would come about, before too long. It might be interesting to note what we have done in this respect. We have had a series of discussions on manpower and educational needs, particularly with the eastern provinces. A special meeting was held; a symposium was held with the representatives of the industry and representatives of the provincial governments, at Pictou, last summer.
Within the next few weeks we shall have on the staff of the Department of Fisheries in Ottawa, for the first time, an educational officer. It is our intention to co-operate with the Department of Labour in its vocational training program, in order to train an adequate number of fishermen and to qualify them to participate in the expansion which is now taking place in the fishing industry, and particularly in our offshore fishing fleet.
We have now in existence three fishing schools on the east coast; one at Pictou, Nova Scotia; one at Caraquet, New Brunswick, and one at Grande Riviere in Quebec. We have the college, or the fishery university at St. John's, Newfoundland.
It is our intention to co-operate with those institutions in order that they be in a position

speechtext:
I am
certainly interested in the introduction of this Bill C-145 to provide for the development of commercial fisheries in Canada. I was particularly interested to hear the minister speak of fresh water fishing and of conferences with the provinces in this connection.
I admire the ambitious program set out in this bill but I hope it will not follow the course of so many actions taken by the Department of Fisheries in the past-the department seems to concentrate all its efforts on the development and promotion of deep sea fisheries, forgetting we have a multi-million dollar fresh water fishing industry in Canada right here in Ontario.
For the past few years fishing along the shores of the Great Lakes has been in dire
March 18, 1966

circumstances. For too long fishermen engaged in this industry have prayed for government intervention both provincial and federal to make it possible for them to maintain this industry. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the stock of fish in the Great Lakes suffered seriously throught the depredations caused by an invasion of lamprey eels. Tremendous efforts were made by the province of Ontario in conjunction with the United States to put an end to this serious situation, and these efforts may have been successful. But there has always been a feeling among fishermen around the Great Lakes that they are the forgotten segment of the industry. They have seen their waters depleted of fish. Moreover, neither the dominion government nor the provincial governments seemed to provide for them the same measures of subsidy or financial assistance as were enjoyed by coastal fishermen.
They have seen the numbers of species of fish in the lakes reduced until at the present time there are only two main varieties of fish which can be taken in any quantity-I speak especially of Lake Erie. These two varieties are perch and smelt, and if it were not for the tremendous efforts of local fishermen in developing a market for these fish the industry around Lake Erie would have passed out of existence.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? I thank the minister for his intervention. I have no quarrel with him there. It may be, as he has said, that this is the situation. But the fact remains that the lakes are being depopulated and tremendous efforts must be made to determine the cause. Some people have attributed it to water pollution. Some attribute it to the development of a particular species which, being cannibal in its nature, is harmful to the young of other species. Various reasons are given, but the fact remains there are fewer fish left each year for fishermen to take and the livelihood of these people depends on the quantity and quality of the fish they are able to catch.
Private Bills
I hope that as a result of this bill aggressive steps will be taken jointly with the province to determine the basic reason for the decline in the fish population. I hope steps will be taken to replenish the lakes with the stock necessary to provide the living to which these fishermen are entitled, having spent their lives in the industry and invested their life savings in equipment.
I understand that the United States government has taken a deep interest in the repopulation of the lakes, and it is my understanding also that some $5 million will this year be spent on this worth-while project. I earnestly hope that our government in conjunction with the province of Ontario will work with the government of the United States to launch a project which will determine once and for all the basic causes of the depletion in fish stocks, and then do something to restock the lakes.
For far too long we have seen the fish hatcheries either working at half their capacity or not working at all. I have seen hatcheries along the lakes shut down completely at a time when the fishermen were worried because they were unable to garner sufficient fish to provide them with a living. This is a serious matter as far as these men are concerned and I am looking forward to this bill having the scope necessary to make it possible for the province of Ontario, the federal government and the fishermen themselves, whose livelihood depends upon it, to do something in accord to settle this basic problem once and for all. These men are in dire straits. They must have help right away.

PROVISION FOR DEFINING LENGTH OF PARLIAMENTARY SESSIONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-6, to provide for the length of sessions of parliament.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-6 was originally prepared and introduced in the last parliament at a time when there was a great deal of discussion about the need for reform of the proceedings and rules of this house. It was never debated in the twenty sixth parliament because it was not reached in private members' hour.
This is a bill to provide for the length of sessions of parliament. Since the first introduction of this bill, a special committee on procedure and organization has made numerous reports as a result of which the rules of the house have been improved and amended in many ways. I personally believe, however, that a great deal of further improvement could be brought to pass if parliament were to plan its sessions and the House of Commons were to plan its sittings, and to fix the normal times of such sittings.
Hon. members may be of the opinion that it is better to look first of all at the forest and then at the trees. I submit if the size of the forest is first determined, then the number and location of the trees can be better determined.
In recognition of the fact that parliament must sit much longer than formerly, to deal with the increasingly complex and numerous matters of public interest, and that this places a great deal of strain on the staff of parliament; in recognition of the fact that ministers of the crown have departmental duties, and all members have constituency duties which must be attended to in periods free of parliamentary duties, I have caused this bill to be re-introduced in this parliament.

I feel that if this bill, or an analogous bill, were enacted, most of the necessary routine work of parliament such as estimates, supply and minor amendments to existing legislation could be programmed for a first mandatory session in each year, and that most legislation bringing in innovations could be given first reading in the mandatory session but could be programmed for the permissive session later in the year.
I submit that this would bring order in the conduct of our business where there is now chaos. This would prevent the use of estimates and interim supply in the annual game of fox and goose played between the house leaders, a game in which they try to outfum-ble each other. This would stop the kind of emotional brinkmanship which creates the atmosphere that even brings down a government, all too unreasonably sometimes to be in the interests of the country.
In clauses 2 and 3 the bill provides for a mandatory session that commences the last Thursday of January and could continue to the second Thursday of September each year. This is the first session of the year, the mandatory session. However, the House of Commons would not normally sit beyond the last Friday of June. The Senate could continue to sit, if it so desires, to finish its business without the pressure that it has now of having to rush in order to meet a House of Commons deadline. The Senate must rise, however, some time before the second Thursday of September, whereupon the session would end. Hon. members should keep clearly in mind, as I am speaking now, the distinction between the session of parliament and the sitting of the House of Commons.
If necessary, and I believe it usually would be, there would be a fall session in which the house would finish sitting on the second Friday of December, at the latest. The Senate could continue to sit until the last Thursday of January in the new year.
Clause 4 of the bill provides for an adjustment of the sittings in an election year, and also for emergency sittings.
Clause 5 provides for a day's debate in the house on the necessity of emergency sittings, if 50 members give notice that they do not consider the call to be one of urgent public importance. This is designed to be preventive and to discourage sittings that are not really necessary and in the public interest. It is also designed to concentrate opposition criticism to one day, rather than have such criticism continue through the sittings.
March 18. 1966

Clause 6 is a very important clause as it provides for government business and private business to be carried over from one session to the next, as if the two sessions were one continuous session. This provision would continue committees, for example, into the next session until their business is completed. Hon. members will appreciate that this would save a great deal of lost time, repetition and expense.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Clause 7 provides that the Speaker and two officials of the House of Commons may, after the house has stopped sitting, complete the formalities of receiving bills from the Senate that have been passed without amendment, without the necessity of the members of the House of Commons attending at the royal assent. This measure would come into force upon royal assent, but would first apply to the year 1967.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, would modernize section 20 of the British North America Act of 1867, 30 Victoria, Chapter 3, which simply provides that there shall be a session of the parliament of Canada once at least every year so that 12 months shall not intervene between the last sitting of the parliament in one session, and the first sitting in the next session.
As our constitution now stands, a prime minister could, in theory, call parliament to sit for one day a year and prorogue it at the end of that day. In practice, of course, a prime minister would, so acting, have great difficulty continuing in office even with recourse to Governor General's warrants. This is an area, however, in which a prime minister has exceptional power and freedom to manoeuvre. This bill, if enacted, would in large measure curtail existing prerogatives of a prime minister. This is not the motivation for this bill, but it would be a result.
Mr. Speaker, most democratic legislative assemblies in the world now have regular dates for the commencement of their sessions, and many spell out the duration of a session with precision. In West Germany the length of sessions generally is fixed by the parliamentarians themselves. There is a so-called steering committee made up of the president-the equivalent of our Speaker-and 30 members of all parties represented, according to their strength in parliament. In each month of a session, one week is devoted to committee work; one week is for the whole
Private Bills
parliament; one week is half committee sessions and half for the whole parliament. The final week is free. The West German parliament normally begins in the first two weeks of October and adjourns at the end of July, with three free weeks at Christmas and two weeks at Easter. These parliamentarians draw up a calendar for each year and spell out precisely the program for the year in respect of it, so that everybody who desires to have dealings in or with parliament has a better opportunity to plan or perform his parliamentary business.
Mr. Speaker, I am not recommending that the West German method be adopted here. I am merely illustrating the businesslike approach of another free legislative assembly.
The bill at hand would initiate the framework within which Canadian parliamentarians, by setting up a joint committee of the house and the other place, could further reform our rules and procedures to meet modern day requirements.

Over the years things have happened to the length of sessions, although so much has happened to the machinery for dealing with this matter. In 1867, in the first parliament when the country was being built and brought together, they met on November 6, 1867 and were through in May the following year. The next session began April 15 and ended June 22. I know they had a tremendous prime minister in those days, but nevertheless there is a contrast all down through the years, and I am not going to take up the time of this crowded house here today to go over all of them.
Even in 1908, at the turn of the century, the session commenced on March 8 and ended on July 13. In the depths of the depression, which in Canada began in 1929 and ended in 1939, in 1932 the third session of the seventeenth parliament, ran from February 4 to May 26. It grappled with the great problems which it had, and a tremendous amount of legislation, some of it of a new kind that was quite shocking, especially to some of the members of the party that was passing it. Then there was the session which commenced on January 17, 1935 and ended on July 5 of that year. This was one of the great dynamic sessions of all times, because this was the famous reform session of R. B. Bennett.
We have found great expansion in the estimates. One has only to compare the figures recently given by the Minister of National Revenue with the few millions of earlier days. We have to recognize, in short, Mr. Speaker, that this now has become a year-round task. No matter how we try to streamline our procedures, a member of the House of Commons of Canada today will find that the whole year must be devoted to his public duties. Now we have, as the mover has mentioned, improved the rules, and the committee and the Speaker in the past parliament deserve great credit.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I think there are many internal improvements which we can yet make. I shall continue to champion the installation of voting machines. As I sit here hour after hour

We could benefit from the situation which exists in other legislatures. As we pass through crises, and we have passed through crises in recent years and in recent days, the mother of parliaments shows the way. Great fundamental issues of monumental concern and of deep emotional content have been met and dealt with in the British parliament in one day, and when the sitting expired the issue was resolved one way or the other.
I like many of the suggestions contained in this bill. I think we have reached the stage where we should know at least, if not where we are at, when we are going to get there, so to speak. We should know in years when there are not elections when the house will meet, when it will adjourn and when, as the hon. member so rightly pointed out, members can be in their constituencies for a good deal of time.
It is my suggestion that sessions should commence in January and have a proper break during July and August. This is where I would be inclined to differ from this measure. It is extremely important that we face up to the fact, as the British have done to a great degree, that we should work on a calendar year with set adjournments, so that our constituents and ourselves can prepare beforehand for a known and sustained period of time when we perform that important part of our work in our constituencies.
Reasonable adjournments at other times, such as at Easter and certainly at Christmas, should be provided. If there is one thing that pains and humiliates me as a member of parliament, it is the dangling of an adjournment before members suggesting that if we get through these, and these, and these-then emerges a great long list of legislation-we might have an adjournment. This is not a sin exclusively of the party how in power. I remember, the suggestions that if we got all the proposed legislation through we would prorogue, if not late in June perhaps in the

middle of July, but we were still telling this to one another on September 1. I think we will have to face up to this fact, Mr. Speaker, as other legislatures have. I am not sure that I am attracted by the West German method. I rather like the idea of committees functioning simultaneously with parliament. I believe that our new system of committees will greatly improve the over-all parliamentary performance.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) who introduced this bill will not feel badly if we tend to give it the "you have got a good idea but we don't like the way you work it out" treatment. I suspect that that will be the verdict of this house during this private members hour.
I should like to join with the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), despite the mistaken way in which he identified me, in saying that I too welcome an effort such as the hon. member for Spadina has made to get us to consider the planning of our parliamentary sessions. He has made it clear in his explanatory notes that this is the purpose of his bill. The member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) made a few references to the time consumed by earlier sessions. He did so by referring to the Parliamentary Guide. However, when you count the precise number of days that parliament sat in some of those earlier sessions, you will see that they were even shorter than appears from the dates given by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie). I only mention this to underline the fact that there has been a tremendous change in the amount of work with which parliament must deal. In the first decade or two sessions of forty and fifty days were long sessions. Now we have enough work to take 150 to 250 days in a year to accomplish. Therefore the problem is with us and there is no use saying that we have to keep on doing things in the same old way. The problems are here and they call for some very real changes.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I would also like to draw attention to the fact that many years ago Dr. Beauchesne, in one of his writings, urged that parliament consider the idea of dividing the session into three parts. If I recall his paper correctly, he suggested that certain formalities such as the address in reply to the speech from the throne and items of that kind might be dealt with in one section of the session; legislation might be dealt with in another and estimates in the third. I forget which of the sections of
March 18. 1966

the session the budget was to be in, but I mention this just to indicate that people who have thought of parliament have had ideas of this nature from time to time, namely that it is not good enough just to go on as they could in the 1870's and 1880's, without any planning. We have come to the point where we have to do some planning of our parliamentary session.
To the extent that the hon. member for Spadina, in introducing this bill, is making us think of this fact, he has done us a service. I also say to him that it is a service to us for him to suggest some precise details. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I think I must point out that in my view some of the details which he suggests are a bit unworkable and would tend to stultify parliament in a way which I think would defeat the hon. member's purpose. When one takes a first look at the bill it looks as though the aim is to have a House of Commons session which begins in January and ends in June, but then the hon. member admits that in most years there would be a second session. So right away the notion that we are going to shorten our sessions is admitted by the hon. member himself to be invalid.
I agree with him that the aim in all of this is not just to shorten our sessions. There is really nothing wrong with our having to work most of the year to do the nation's business. But what we should be aiming at is the efficient use of the time we spend here. As I say, the hon. member immediately admits that what he proposes as the exception, namely a second session each year, is likely to become the rule.
Then I should point out to him that in his bill he has so many deadlines that I think we would find ourselves doing what we have already done to the Electoral Boundaries Act. We very solemnly passed in the last parliament legislation regarding electoral boundaries and we put into that legislation a provision as to what parliament must do. We said that members of parliament must debate any objections members have within a fixed number of days from a certain point. I think that is the first example, in recent times at any rate, of putting into a statute what parliament must do.
What have we done with that legislation, Mr. Speaker? We passed a bill through all three readings very quickly, and then the Senators did the same thing, just to change that deadline. X would suspect that if the hon. member's bill went through in its present
Private Bills
form with its various deadlines we would find ourselves at each and every session of parliament, both in the main session and in the second session, having to pass bills to amend the basic law relating to the sessions, so that we could do what needed to be done under the circumstances.
Therefore I think that the idea of fixing a precise calendar schedule by statute is one which would be pretty hard to stick to in the free kind of parliament that we have. After all, we are not just a business organization of the kind which can program its work as though we were turning it over to a computer. We are a living organization representing the life of the Canadian people as it exists in 1966 or 1967. The things which will happen and the needs which will arise create differing situations, and if we try to deal with all of them in a timed program which has been restricted and stultified, then I fear we would get into difficulty.
I do not say these things critically as though the hon. member should not have put these ideas into this bill. After all, he can come back to me and say that we have certain restrictions now. For example, we sit at 2.30 in the afternoon and quit at ten at night, except for the late show. We sit at eleven o'clock on Friday mornings and quit at six. We do not sit on Saturdays or Sundays. So we already have a great many restrictions. But so far as our work is concerned, a good deal of it is determined by the program which the government brings in and by the reaction of the opposition to the legislative program. I believe this necessitates a certain amount of freedom on the part of the House of Commons during the session to deal with its work as the situation seems to demand.
Having said this, having been critical of the hon. member's precise program, I want to come back and say I welcome the idea that parliament should discuss the planning of its work. I think we should take another look at Dr. Beauchesne's suggestion of some years ago of dividing the session into two, three or four parts and trying to see whether we can deal with some of the work in one part of the session, certain work in another part, and so on.
I also think-and here I hope my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) will not mind if I disagree with him-that if we are going to plan our work there is something else we must do. I think we have to look at the importance, and I think the potentially greater importance, of our committee work.

If we are to do this, then where I disagree with my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) is that I think we will have to provide time in the parliamentary year when committees can sit when the House of Commons itself is not in session. I have twice had the experience in the years I have been here of being on committees which sat when parliament was not actually in session, and it is my judgment that the committees which sit under those circumstances have a much better chance to do an effective job than committees which sit while the house is actually in session.
I am not suggesting that we take away from the executive any of the powers it has as far as legislation is concerned, but I am suggesting that committees could be upstaged and be given more importance and more work to do. This question was discussed last year or the year before in connection with our changes in the rules. Some misunderstanding developed; some people thought we were trying to arrange for holiday time, or what-have-you. I hope that those misunderstandings can be resolved and that we can take another look at this whole question of upgrading our committee work as part of the planning of the whole session.
I emphasize the fact that, in my view, this is probably the answer to our present problem, because we have so much more work to do now than we had 30, 40 or 100 years ago. Some of us have already talked about the length of sessions, which was six or seven weeks at the beginning of this country's history. I may say that the sessions really did not get lengthy until the second world war. Even the long sessions complained about just before the first world war were sessions which, in terms of total length of time, did not amount to more than six or seven months, or 25 or 26 weeks out of the 52.
We have much more work to do now because the amount of money we must consider has multiplied manyfold. We no longer deal as a parliament just with post offices, roads and defence. We deal with everything which affects our lives from the cradle to the grave. We go under the earth, into the sea, and we are concerned with outer space. Everything concerns us. I think it is unrealistic to think that, without any change in the rules or any changes in the matters we handle, we can do everything right here on the same floor in the same procedural structure in which we conducted our business 85 to 90 years ago in a matter of six or seven weeks.

To me the answer is not to pass the excess work to the executive or to the bureaucracy. To me the answer is to make greater use of our committees structure. But I plead the point that we are not going to get the full advantage out of our new committees structure, with smaller numbers on committees and so on, if we continue having committees sit while the house is in session. To me this is one of the major matters, as I say, which we should look at in connection with the whole business of planning our parliamentary year.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Obviously I could go on but I see the clock is moving and I think others should have the chance to speak. I will sit down by saying that even though I find many flaws in the details of the bill presented by the hon. member for Spadina and he will agree with me that he does not want to end up by stultifying the parliamentary year nevertheless, he has done us a service, by making us think about planning our parliamentary year. I hope that we will get around to planning it soon.

I know that this would have been difficult these past few years because of the many sudden elections.
1 think that, in addition to determining the length of parliamentary sessions, this would exclude the risk of elections during the four years of the life of a parliament, and therefore it would be much easier to apply the bill introduced this afternoon by the member for Spadina.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few personal comments on the bill now before us, that is Bill No. C-6, an act to provide for the length of sessions of parliament.
As pointed out by the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Spadina, the purpose of this measure is to set definite dates for the opening and length of sessions. As a matter of fact, the bill provides as the opening date the last Thursday of January and as the closing date for the House of Commons, the last Friday of June. The bill also provides for an Easter recess of at least five days and the possibility of a second session in September.
At first sight at least, there can be no doubt that it would be quite desirable to limit the length of sessions and especially to know beforehand and with certainty the schedule of future sessions.
As one of the previous speakers said, sessions are getting longer because of the increasing complexity of the problems considered by the house.
A quick review of the parliamentary history of our nation shows that, in the first years of confederation, the sessions lasted between two and two and a half months. The 1912-13 session went on for six and a half months, but it was at the time of the famous debate on the naval forces bill. Of course, that session was an exception to the rule.
During the first world war, the sessions lasted about four months.
During the second world war, Parliament began to sit all year round, but sessions were broken by adjournments.
In fact, at the time of the second world war, Parliament did not sit more than six months per year. But since that time, the length of the sessions has grown constantly and we now sit almost the year round, except when we take holidays to go electioneering.
It is to be hoped that this type of holiday will not occur too soon.
It is, therefore, expedient to study the problem, to examine the bill and the reasons for setting definite limits to the length of sessions.
Private Bills
Mr. Speaker, I believe the role of a member does not only consist in sitting in the house, taking part in debates and working in committees; a member must also be the spokesman of his constituents. It is very difficult for him to perform this duty and to carry out this most important task effectively if he does not have the opportunity to understand their needs fully and to consider their views. Therefore, a member must have, as far as possible, some spare time to meet with his constituents, discuss with them and, at times, live among them several weeks during the year.
I believe the interests of democracy would be better served if hon. members could keep in touch constantly with their constituents and, especially if definite periods were set aside every year to allow them, not to take a holiday, but to pay a visit to their constituents.
Adjournments at definite dates, as proposed in this bill, would also allow ministers to catch their breath and to visit their own ridings as well as to prepare long-term programs for their department.
Mr. Strathearn Gordon published some years ago a rather interesting book entitled Our Parliament.
It deals, of course, with the British parliament at Westminster, but his remarks can be applied as well to our own parliament in Ottawa. And I quote, Mr. Speaker- [English]
I quote from page 58 of Our Parliament by Strathearn Gordon:
Another subject which is often raised is the length of the session. Why don't M.P.'s work for more than eights months in the year? The answer is that they do-but not at Westminster. Most Ministers undoubtedly look forward to the 'holidays', when they are free from parliamentary cares, as the periods when they can put their best work into their Departments. But for ordinary Members, too, reasonably long adjournments are a practical necessity. When a man has for many weeks been living a sort of double life, spending late nights at Westminster, speaking in his constituency at the weekends, working in the train in between, with his private affairs neglected and his nerves in shreds, it is surely right to allow him time to recuperate and think. Three hundred and seventy years ago the Lord Keeper was expressing the idea in almost lyrical style:
There the author goes on to quote the Lord Keeper:
The sessions (he said) cannot be long; by reason of the springtime, 'tis fit that gentlemen should repair to their countries; the justices of assize also to go to their circuits.
So the good hours should not be lost in idle speeches, but the little time we have should be bestowed wholly on such businesses as are needful to be considered of.

March 18, 1966

Finally the author quotes also the great parliamentarian himself, Sir Winston Churchill:
If you wish to say what is wrong with Parliament ... it is that it sits far too long in the year. I would lay down that except in times of war or great national emergency Parliament should not sit more than five months, with the ordinary short intervals, say, occupying six months of the year. That ought to be the maximum.

speechtext:
For some years the French Government has stressed on many occasions, both publicly and in conversations with Allied governments, its view that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization no longer meets, as far as the French Government is concerned, the conditions which prevail in the world at the present time and which are basically different from those prevailing in 1949 and the following years.
2.	In fact, the threat which weighed upon the Western world, particularly in Europe and which was the reason for the conclusion of the Treaty has changed in nature. It no longer presents the immediate and menacing character it once had. At the same time, the European countries have restored their economies and, as a consequence, are recovering their former strength. France in particular is developing an atomic armament, which, by its very nature, precludes its integration. In the third place, the nuclear balance between the Soviet Union and the United States of America which has replaced the monopoly held by the latter, has transformed the general conditions of Western defence. Finally, it is a fact that Europe is no longer the center of international crises. This center has moved elsewhere, notably to Asia, where the Atlantic Alliance countries are as a whole nof evidently involved.
3.	This evolution in no way leads the French Government to question the Treaty signed in Washington on April 4, 1949. In other words, and barring developments which, in the years to come, might basically modify relations between east and west, it does not intend to avail itself in 1969 of the provisions of Article 13 of the Treaty, and it considers that the Alliance should remain in being as long as the need appears evident.
4.	The above position having been stated unequivocally the problem of the Organization itself arises, that is to say all agreements, arrangements and decisions subsequent to the signing of the Treaty, whether they be multilateral or bilateral in form. The French Government considers that this Organization no longer corresponds to what in its opinion seems to be required.
5.	One could undoubtedly have envisaged that negotiations could have been undertaken to modify by common consent the provisions
in force. The French Government would have been happy to propose this had it had reason to believe that such negotiations would have led to the result it has in mind. Unfortunately everything indicates that such an attempt would be doomed to fail since all of France's partners seem or profess openly to favour maintaining the status quo, or reinforcing all that which is henceforth unacceptable from the French point of view.
6.	France accordingly is led to recognize the consequences for it in this situation and to take the measures which seem required and which in its opinion are not in the least incompatible with its participation in the Alliance, nor in military operations with its Allies should the need arise. Already in the past the French Government has taken steps of this nature with regard to its naval forces serving with NATO whether in the Mediterranean or in the Atlantic. What is now in question are its land and air forces stationed in Germany and assigned to the Allied Command in Europe. France intends to bring their assignment to an end. This decision will entail France's simultaneous withdrawal from the two integrated commands under which its forces are serving and to which it is contributing within the framework of NATO, i.e. the Supreme Allied Command in Europe and the Central Europe Command, and consequently the transfer of the headquarters for these two commands outside French territory. The implementation of all these measures raises of course a number of problems, which the French Government is now prepared to discuss with its allies. There will be a need to consider the liaison which should be established between the French Command and NATO Command as well as to determine the conditions under which French forces, particularly in Germany, would participate in wartime, should Article 5 of the Washington Treaty be evoked, in joint military actions, with reference to Command and operations themselves. This implies in particular that French land and air forces which are stationed at present in Germany would be maintained in that country under the agreements of October 23, 1954. This for its part the French Government is disposed to do.
7.	Consideration should be given, on the other hand, to problems which may present

themselves to France with regard to the Military Committee and the Standing Group, including the problem of liaison between these bodies and the French Command.
8.	Such are the broad outlines of measures contemplated by the French Government which it regards as necessary to adapt to new conditions the modalities of its participation in the Atlantic Alliance. It is prepared to enter discussions with regard to the implementation of these measures, and it hopes that appropriate arrangements may be agreed upon by all its Allies.
9.	Multilateral problems are not however the only ones to be considered as far as Canada and France are concerned. Both countries have concluded agreements in the past concerning the construction and the operation of airports on French territory intended for the use of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
10.	The French Government considers that these agreements no longer meet present conditions, which lead it to recover the full exercise of its sovereignty on French territory, or in other words no longer to accept that foreign units, installations or bases in France should in any way be responsible to authorities other than French. It is ready to examine, and eventually to settle with the Government of Canada, the practical consequences this policy entails.
11.	Moreover the French Government is ready to discuss the military facilities which could be placed at the disposal of the Government of Canada on French territory in the event of a conflict to which both countries would participate under the Atlantic Alliance. These facilities could be the object of an Agreement to be concluded between both Governments.
Monday, March 21, 1966
